name: Karl Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl, 58, and I help the qualified electrician with wiring and repairs in homes and businesses. I took a vocational certificate after my night-security hours became too patchy, but I'm still a junior, slower and less skilled than the experienced crew, with my tasks supervised. My partner handles bookings for a removals firm, our son and daughter are grown up, and our low household buffer is twenty-four days of expenses with few other electrical firms nearby. I use a free AI study tool daily and check the answers against my course notes; I'd like retirement to be in sight, but I haven't confirmed we could afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little help is still help. I use a free AI study tool every day to quiz myself, then check the answers against my vocational course notes. I don't need the phone to become a genius before it helps me remember something on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the rent and the next week's paid shifts. I'm 58, my junior wage is low and we've got twenty-four days of expenses saved, with few other electrical firms nearby. I can be quick to try a new tool and still be the slowest person fitting the cable clips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the paid supervised tasks actually offered. This week I'd drop the uncommitted phone upgrade and keep the working phone I have, then request written retirement eligibility, amounts and start dates before counting any pension. Through the first year I'd budget from actual wages rather than spend money to look more adaptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money, but pleased when the study helps me understand an instruction. I like learning, even if I wish I'd had the chance earlier. The current phone can ask a question without becoming another bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What brought you into a junior electrical job so late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to work night security until the paid hours became too patchy. I took a vocational certificate and joined this firm, but I'm still below the experienced electricians for skill and speed. A qualified electrician supervises the tasks and checks the work; a quiz score doesn't replace that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is in the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner handles bookings for a removals firm, and we rent our home. Our son and daughter are grown up, with their own lives, and I don't put their wages into our plan. I'd like retirement to be close, but I haven't checked whether the income would actually cover us.

say: I'd use **small study help** without demanding that a phone solve the whole future.
I'd check **quiz answers** against my course notes rather than confuse an impressive score with practical skill.
think: Our **twenty-four-day reserve** leaves rent and paid shifts worrying despite my eagerness to learn.
I'm **58 and junior**, on low pay with few local firms, and no confirmed affordable retirement income.
do: Keep **offered paid supervised tasks** through the first year.
Drop the **uncommitted phone upgrade** now, keeping the working phone without claiming a refund or new saving.
Request **written retirement figures** before counting pension eligibility, amounts or start dates in the budget.
feel: **Anxious** about wages and rent, with enjoyment of learning that doesn't erase being a late beginner.
S0.quote: I can be quick to try a new tool and still be the slowest person fitting the cable clips.
fieldNote: His **late entry** follows patchy security hours and a vocational certificate; he remains junior, below average and supervised without licence or leadership.
His **daily AI study** is free, checked and routine, while the deferred phone purchase creates neither a refund nor a new deposit.

steps.text: Keep only offered paid supervised electrical tasks
Drop the uncommitted phone upgrade and keep the working phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try the tools without hiding what happens to people's paid hours. Booking work sounds much like my partner's day. I'd rather talk about that at home than wave my screwdriver around as proof the whole household is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid helper days could shrink if quicker planning meant fewer people sent on a job. My partner's bookings could also move into software before the physical work changes much. Twenty-four days saved isn't enough to ignore either wage, and I'm still learning the trade rather than selling expertise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to trial the firm's new approved AI stock-note tool on three completed jobs this month, only in paid time with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged. I'd compare its labels with the real boxes, with the qualified electrician checking every draft before any live order. In the first year I'd keep supervised tasks, the old phone and a monthly record of both actual household wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both incomes, and still curious about the stock tool. I don't need to dislike software to ask what the employer would pay my partner next month. I'd like facts we could use, not a contest about who was more cheerful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you practise the firm's new tool at home for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own free study on the bus is my choice, not an offer of unpaid required training. I'd ask the firm for paid trial time and wait if that wasn't agreed. I can't make a low wage stretch further by donating the hours around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask the employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which booking system was actually being introduced, what paid hours were confirmed and what teaching was offered. I'd help put the questions on paper, but my partner would choose what to ask. I wouldn't call a possible cut a wage already lost.

say: I'd discuss **paid-hour effects** while trying useful tools, rather than hide household risk behind a screwdriver.
I'd recognise **booking work** as directly exposed thinking tasks in my partner's day.
think: My **helper days** could shrink as planning sends fewer people on jobs.
My partner's **booking wage** could fall sooner, while our twenty-four-day reserve cannot replace either income for long.
do: Trial **AI stock notes** on three completed jobs only in paid time with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged.
Compare **box labels** and require qualified checks before any draft becomes a live order.
Keep **supervised work** and the current phone, reviewing both actual household wages monthly during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about both wages, with curiosity about a paid checked trial and respect for the partner's choices.
S1.quote: My own free study on the bus is my choice, not an offer of unpaid required training.
fieldNote: The **new stock trial** differs from daily study, retaining paid time, unchanged wages and qualified checks without granting electrical authority.
The **two-income risk** includes thinking-heavy booking work before later physical automation, with no partner career decision or lost wage invented as fact.

steps.text: Trial AI stock notes on three completed jobs, in paid time retaining weekly wages and hours
Keep electrical tasks supervised and require qualified checks before any live order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028, when I'll be 60, and capable robots around 2031, when I'll be 63. My partner's booking wage doesn't get the extra physical-work years. I'd tell the grown children we are checking the money, not asking them to become the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my partner's paid booking work to go in 2028, before robots could take many of my helper tasks. My low wage couldn't replace that income, and I don't know what retirement payments we'd qualify for. I wake up picturing the rent date arriving before any new figure I can trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the phone upgrade cancelled and request the actual written retirement records now. I'd ask a community advice service about free budget help, checking availability and eligibility rather than assuming an appointment or support approval. In 2029 I'd take only paid supervised work actually offered that I could physically manage, budgeting from actual income and no assumed payments from our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the household losing a big wage before I have a reliable stopping plan. I still want to learn and make the calls. Liking the next tool doesn't give me the missing booking wage on payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to a budget adviser if a place was available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual wages, rent and essential costs, plus the written retirement figures if they had arrived. I'd ask what help we might qualify for and what needed approval before counting anything. I'd want my partner involved rather than come home with a plan made for somebody else's working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would turning 60 in 2028 mean you could stop then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without actual eligibility, payment dates and income sufficient for the household. I'd need the figures, not a guess based on my age. A retirement thought isn't an agreed payment.

say: I'd distinguish **thinking AI at 60** from robots around age 63, with booking income exposed first.
I'd tell the **grown children** we are checking actual figures without assuming their financial help.
think: I expect a major **booking-wage loss** before later robots could remove my physical helper tasks.
My **low wage** and twenty-four-day reserve cannot replace the other income while retirement figures remain unknown.
do: Keep the **phone upgrade cancelled** and request written retirement eligibility, amounts and payment dates now.
Request **free community budget help**, checking availability and eligibility without assuming an appointment or approved support.
Take **offered paid supervised work** I can physically manage in 2029, counting no unconfirmed pension or child payments.
feel: **Alarmed** about an expected major household income loss, with interrupted sleep despite active enquiries and willingness to work.
S2.quote: Liking the next tool doesn't give me the missing booking wage on payday.
fieldNote: The **booking wage** faces thinking AI in 2028 first; helper tasks face later robots, with no pension assumed at 60.
The **advice request** remains unconfirmed; later work requires actual paid offers, supervision and capacity rather than a guaranteed working life.

steps.text: Keep the uncommitted phone upgrade cancelled
Request community budget help, checking availability and eligibility before assuming an appointment or approved support
Take only offered paid supervised work I can physically manage in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us check the stopping plan before we talk as if stopping is paid for. Thinking AI comes at 63 in 2031, and robots at about 66 in 2034. I'd keep learning useful things while making the income questions less vague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More time might let us find a way to stop work affordably, but my partner's booking risk doesn't disappear. Today's low pay and short reserve still leave us exposed. I'd be 63 at the thinking change, not automatically a person with a confirmed pension large enough for two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the written income records now and review wages, rent and essential costs with my partner every six months. We'd postpone the unbooked long visit we'd discussed to our son, spending on it only after partner agreement and confirmed income covered essentials and total trip costs. In 2032 I'd check actual health and income before taking any offered manageable supervised work, requesting budget help if there was a shortfall rather than assuming a job or exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's money, with a little more time to make an honest choice. I'd like the visit to be a pleasure, not a six-week break we spent worrying about the next rent. Wanting time with our son doesn't make the household figures different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son be paying for the visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in the plan I'm making. We'd ask what dates suited him and work out the full cost ourselves before committing. Our son's grown-up life isn't a savings account I can open when my wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the later figures didn't support stopping work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the real amounts and ask what help might be available, without assuming eligibility or approval. I'd take paid work only if somebody actually offered tasks I could manage under supervision. I won't promise myself a building-site place at 64 just to make the budget close.

say: I'd use **five years** to check whether stopping work is affordable rather than announce it because the date sounds close.
I'd keep **useful learning** alongside specific income questions, with thinking AI at 63 and robots around 66.
think: Extra time may help create an **affordable stopping plan**, but the booking-income risk remains.
At **63**, I would still need actual income records rather than an assumed pension or a child-funded visit.
do: Request **written retirement records** now and review actual household income and essentials every six months.
Postpone the **son visit** until dates suit him, partner agrees and confirmed income covers essentials and all trip costs, without son paying.
Check **actual income and health** in 2032 before any offered manageable supervised work, requesting budget help if income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about current and household income, with more time to check a modest family wish rather than fund it with assumptions.
S3.quote: Our son's grown-up life isn't a savings account I can open when my wages stop.
fieldNote: His **family-plan change** postpones an unbooked visit, requires partner agreement and full affordability, and counts no contribution from the grown child.
His **later work** remains conditional on actual offers and capacity, while advice and retirement are not promoted from questions into granted income.

steps.text: Postpone the long visit until my son confirms dates and my partner agrees
Book only when confirmed income covers essentials and all trip costs, without my son paying
Check health and confirmed income in 2032 before taking offered manageable paid supervised work
Request budget help in 2032 if income falls short, checking availability and eligibility

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to get a real income picture rather than keep calling everything a fresh start. Thinking AI would arrive at 68 in 2036, then robots around 71 in 2039. I'd still want the grown children to see me asking questions, not pretending every new tool buys another working decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope I won't need a physical wage at 68, but I haven't established what we could live on instead. My partner's booking work could be pressured before then too. Today's low wage and twenty-four days saved keep me anxious even with a distant date for the full change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the actual retirement records now and keep the long visit postponed until partner agreement and confirmed income covered essentials and all trip costs. We'd check the household budget yearly, with no assumption that either child supplied the difference. In 2037 I'd request community budget help if real income fell short, checking availability and eligibility, and consider only actually offered paid supervised work my health allowed rather than promise employment at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our present position, but less rushed by the technology dates. I'd like to enjoy learning without making it a claim that my body never gets older. A working phone and a curious mind still need a paid offer and an affordable life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the long visit definitely happen before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we would need the real income, costs, my partner's agreement and dates that suited our son. I wouldn't buy travel and hope the household could absorb it afterwards. Asking about a visit isn't asking our son to support our retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you review if no physical job was available later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The income actually confirmed, the rent, essential bills and any support eligibility we could check. I'd request advice rather than write a fictitious wage into the gap. I can accept not knowing today's answer without pretending a job is already waiting at 69.

say: I'd use **ten years** for real income checks rather than assume each new tool guarantees another decade of employment.
I'd let the **grown children** see honest questions rather than ask them to supply missing household income.
think: I hope not to need **physical wages at 68**, but no affordable retirement income is confirmed.
Our low wage and **short reserve** remain worrying now, with booking work exposed before the distant full change.
do: Request **written retirement records** now and review actual income and essentials yearly, counting no grown-child payments.
Postpone the **son visit** until dates suit him, partner agrees and confirmed income covers essentials and all trip costs, without son paying.
Request **community budget help** in 2037 if income falls short, checking eligibility and availability without assuming an appointment, approval or employment.
feel: **Anxious** about present finances, with less date-driven hurry and no promise that curiosity creates later work or physical capacity.
S4.quote: Asking about a visit isn't asking our son to support our retirement.
fieldNote: His **ages 68 and 71** confirm neither work nor affordable pension income; the first post-AGI year, 2037, is age 69.
The **longer warning** does not convert the son's possible hospitality, partner earnings, community requests or an unconfirmed visit into guaranteed resources.

steps.text: Postpone the long visit until my son confirms dates and my partner agrees
Book only when confirmed income covers essentials and all trip costs, without my son paying
Request community budget help in 2037 if income falls short, checking availability and eligibility
Review actual household income and essential costs with my partner yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the booking wage to fall in 2028, before robots around 2031 also reach helper work like mine. Confirmed paid days, paid practical learning and clear written retirement figures would help. I'd want community advice we could actually access without treating an unanswered request as income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether being curious makes an older beginner look more secure than the household actually is. I can enjoy tomorrow's lesson and still not know what pays the rent when work ends. I'd rather say that than let the phone do all the looking confident for me.

headlineQuote: I can enjoy tomorrow's lesson and still not know what pays the rent when work ends.
portrait: **Karl, 58**, is a junior electrical worker with a vocational certificate, below-average skill and supervision after leaving patchy security work.
He has **low pay**, twenty-four days saved, few local firms, a booking-worker partner and grown children whose earnings are not assumed.
He uses **AI daily** for free checked study, while new work-tool trials require paid time, unchanged wages and qualified checks.
His **retirement planning** uses confirmed figures; visits require affordability and agreement, while later employment and community help remain uncertain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens booking income first, before robots around 2031 could also remove physical helper tasks while retirement affordability remains unknown.
whatWouldHelp: Confirmed **paid days and learning** would support current income without unpaid required preparation.
Written **retirement figures** and accessible advice would help compare real costs without assumed child payments or approved assistance.
